Chapter I · Hario V60

THE 4:6 METHOD


🏆 TETSU KASUYA — 2016 WORLD BREWERS CUP CHAMPION (JAPAN)
☕ 20 g coffee💧 300 g water ⚖ 1 : 15🌡 93 °C⚙ medium-coarse
0:00Pour 60 g — the bloom. Let it breathe.
0:45Pour 60 g (scale reads 120 g). First 40% done — this half sets sweetness & acidity.
1:30Pour 60 g (180 g). Now the 60% — this half sets strength & body.
2:10Pour 60 g (240 g).
2:40Pour 60 g (300 g). Drawdown should finish ≈ 3:30.
The trick: grind coarser than you think. Each pour should fully drain before the next. → tuning chart overleaf!
src: honestcoffeeguide.com/brew-recipes/tetsu-kasuya-4-6-method · kurasu.kyoto (champion story)

Chapter I · Hario V60

TUNING THE 4:6

Play with the first 120 g (2 pours) to steer taste:
40+80Sweeter, less acidity
60+60Balanced (the standard)
80+40Brighter, more acidity
Then split the last 180 g to steer strength:
1 pourLighter body, tea-like & clean
2 poursMedium strength — balanced cup
3 poursFuller body, strongest cup

Chapter I · Hario V60

THE ULTIMATE V60


🏆 JAMES HOFFMANN — 2007 WORLD BARISTA CHAMPION (UK)
☕ 30 g coffee💧 500 g water ⚖ 60 g/L🌡 100 °C, just off boil⚙ medium-fine☕☕ serves 2
0:00Bloom with 60 g (2× the dose) and give the brewer a good swirl.
0:45Pour 240 g steadily (scale reads 300 g) — aim to finish by ~1:15.
1:15Centre-pour 200 g more, slow and gentle (500 g total).
1:45Stir once each direction with a spoon to knock grounds off the wall, then swirl 2–3 times.
3:30Drawdown done — flat bed = even cup. Probably the most-watched pour-over recipe on the internet.
One kettle, no fuss, hard to get wrong. The swirls do the work that fancy pouring usually does.
src: honestcoffeeguide.com/brew-recipes/james-hoffmann-v60 · timer.coffee
5
Chapter I · Hario V60

THE NEW 10-POUR


🏆 TETSU KASUYA AGAIN — HIS NEW MULTI-POUR (2026)
☕ 20 g coffee💧 300 g water ⚖ 1 : 15🌡 95–96 °C⚙ SUPER coarse (40–45 clicks C40!) ⚙ our Chestnut C5 ESP: ~80–90 clicks ≈ 1.6.0–1.8.0
0:00Pour 30 g — the bloom gets the only long rest: 30 seconds.
0:30Then a steady drumbeat: +30 g every 15 seconds — nine more pours.
2:30Last pour lands (300 g on the scale).
3:30Drawdown done.
The anti-4:6, from the 4:6 man himself: much coarser, hotter, double the pours — chasing syrupy body & sweetness instead of balance. His logic: “specialty coffee is additive, not subtractive.” Goes almost jelly-thick as it cools!
our verdict vs the 4:6:

Chapter I · Hario V60

THE FIVE-POUR


🏆 MATT WINTON — 2021 WORLD BREWERS CUP CHAMPION
☕ 20 g coffee💧 300 g water ⚖ 1 : 15🌡 93 °C → 88 °C⚙ medium
1.Five equal pours of 60 g. First pour at 93 °C — wet everything evenly.
2.Pour from a height — the agitation is the technique. No stirring, no swirling.
3.Wait ~30 s between pours, or until the bed runs dry / dripping nearly stops.
4.Later pours at 88 °C (he used two kettles!).
5.Final drawdown ~3:30. Total ≈ 6:50. Inhale before you sip.
Bitter & dry → grind coarser. Sour & thin → grind finer. The anti-4:6: height and splash instead of gentle spirals.
src: honestcoffeeguide.com/brew-recipes/matt-winton-v60-five-pour

Chapter II · AeroPress

CHAMPION'S RECIPE


🏆 WENDELIEN VAN BUNNIK — 2019 WORLD AEROPRESS CHAMPION (NL)
☕ 30 g coffee💧 100 g water 🌡 92 °C⚙ med-fine (EK43 @ 7)🙃 inverted
0:00AeroPress inverted. Pour 100 g water over the coffee (~10 s).
0:10Stir 20 times in ~10 seconds. Vigorous but loving.
0:20Rinse filter, lock the cap on.
0:40Flip her over, press everything out.
~1:00Done — an intense little cup. Dilute with hot water to taste.
A one-minute brew that took the world title. Strong dose, tiny water, big stir — the opposite of everything "safe."
src: bigcupofcoffee.com/winning-aeropress-champion-recipes · aeropress.com/pages/wac-recipes
9
Chapter II · AeroPress

THE ULTIMATE (DAILY) AEROPRESS


☕ JAMES HOFFMANN — THE EVERYDAY ONE
☕ 11 g coffee💧 200 g water 🌡 just off boil⚙ fine – med-fine🙂 upright
0:00No filter rinse needed. Add coffee, pour all 200 g at once.
0:15Insert the plunger just into the top — it stops the dripping.
2:00Steep done — hold brewer + plunger, swirl gently. No vortex! Just settle the crust.
2:30After 30 s rest, press slowly for ~30 seconds, all the way.
3:00Done. Cooler water for darker roasts.
The lazy-perfect morning cup — one pour, one swirl, one press. Our weekday default?
src: fluentincoffee.com/james-hoffmann-aeropress
10
Chapter II · AeroPress

ICED AEROPRESS


🧊 JAMES HOFFMANN — FLASH-CHILLED
☕ 22 g coffee💧 240 g water @ 100 °C 🧊 160 g ice in the server⚙ finer end of medium🙂 upright
prepWeigh 160 g of ice into the vessel you'll press into. AeroPress on top.
0:00Pour all 240 g of hot water. Plunger in to hold the vacuum.
4:00Swirl the brewer, then rest 30 seconds.
4:30Press gently, straight onto the ice.
doneSwirl until the ice is gone, serve over fresh cubes.
Same trick as the flash brew: the ice is the missing brew water. Long hot steep + instant chill = big flavour, zero dilution guilt.
src: aeroprecipe.com/recipes/james-hoffmann-iced-aeropress

12
Chapter II · AeroPress

THE REIGNING RECIPE

🏆 GEORGE STANICA — 2024 WORLD AEROPRESS CHAMPION 🇷🇴
☕ 18 g coffee💧 ~100 g brew + dilution🌡 96 °C⚙ 870 µm🙃 inverted
ON OUR C5 ESP: 58 clicks. His C40 Red Clix at 58 clicks is stated as 870 µm; ours is ≈15 µm/click, so 870 ÷ 15 lands on the same number. Medium-coarse (p. 50).
0:00Inverted. 1 rinsed filter in the cap, set aside. Coffee in, pour ~50 g at 96 °C.
0:00–0:30Bloom 30 seconds. Let it swell and breathe.
0:30Pour the second ~50 g. Cap on.
1:35Flip and press — slow, 30–40 seconds. Stop at the hiss.
~2:15You'll have 76–79 g of concentrate. Now the important part →
diluteAdd warm water to 130–135 g total, then 20–30 g room-temperature water. That last cold splash is the whole trick — it drops the cup straight into the drinking window and lifts the aromatics.
George's own words: this was tailored to one specific coffee and roast — adapt it to your palate. He's a software engineer who brews on weekends. Hope for all of us.
★ Start here if you've never brewed a competition recipe. Standard gear, no sifting, no second server — a bloom, a press, a clever dilution.
worldaeropresschampionship.com/pages/1st-george-stanica-romania-2024
13
Chapter II · AeroPress

THE NEWEST CHAMPION

🏆 NEMO POP — 2025 WORLD AEROPRESS CHAMPION 🇦🇺
☕ 18 g coffee💧 100 g brew + 70 g bypass🌡 84 °C⚙ sifted @ 200 µm🙂 upright
Her grinder: Comandante Trailmaster x25, Tigershark burrs, 31 clicks, sifted at 200 µm. No micron figure was published, so I can't convert it honestly — start at 48 clicks on the C5 and tune. Water was 125 ppm, bypass at 50 °C.
prepPour 70 g of 50 °C bypass water into the carafe first. Yes — before you brew.
grindGrind slowly, blow off the chaff, sift the fines out. Two AeroPress micro-filters in a Flow Control Cap.
0:00AeroPress upright on the carafe. Coffee in. Pour 100 g at 84 °C, wetting every ground.
0:25Stir "NSNS–WEWE" — north-south twice, then east-west twice. A cross, not a swirl.
0:50Begin pressing gently, for about 20 seconds.
1:10Serve. The brew lands on the waiting bypass water.
What's radical: 84 °C is cold by any normal standard, and the bypass water waits in the cup rather than going in after. Champions keep drifting cooler and sweeter.
⚠ Needs a Flow Control Cap, micro-filters and a sieve. Without them: upright, 84 °C, one paper filter, press slowly — you'll get most of the way there.
aeropress.com/blogs/w-a-c-aeropress-recipes/1st-nemo-pop-australia-2025
14
Chapter II · AeroPress

THE DOUBLE BREW

🏆 TAY WIPVASUTT — 2023 WORLD AEROPRESS CHAMPION 🇹🇭
☕ 18 g (16 + 2)💧 149 g @ 89 °C🌡 89 °C📄 3 filters!🙂 upright
The strangest recipe in the book: he brews the coffee twice, pouring the first brew back through a fresh second dose. You'll want two servers and a chopstick. Grind wasn't published — start medium-fine, ~40 clicks.
setupThree standard paper filters in the cap. Chamber on server #1. 16 g coffee in.
0:00Pour 55 g of 89 °C water.
0:25–0:30Stir 5 seconds, then insert the plunger for immersion.
0:45–0:55Press 10 seconds. You'll get ~35 g of liquid.
1:05Move onto server #2. Pull the plunger, add 2 g more coffee, pour 50 g hot water.
1:30–1:35Stir 5 seconds with a chopstick. Now pour the first brew back in. Plunger in.
2:10–2:20Press 10 seconds.
diluteRoom-temp water to 110 g total, then hot water to 154 g. Serve.
Why it works: the second pass runs already-brewed coffee over fresh grounds — sweetness and body without the bitter tail. Three filters slow it down and polish the cup clean.
aeropress.com/blogs/w-a-c-aeropress-recipes/1st-tay-wipvasutt-thailand-2023 (non-inverted version)
15
Chapter II · AeroPress

THE COLD-WATER SCHOOL

Two champions who won by refusing to use hot water. If you only try one experiment this month, make it this one.
🏆 TUOMAS MERIKANTO — 2021 CHAMPION 🇫🇮 · 80 °C
☕ 18 g💧 50 g + 150 g🌡 80 °C🙃 inverted
0:00Inverted. Pour 50 g at 80 °C. Stir.
0:05Pour the remaining 150 g. Stir again.
0:20Cap on, flip, and press for ~20 seconds.
A forty-second brew at kettle-has-been-sitting temperature. It should be thin and sour by every rule we know. It isn't — it's sweet and clean, because 80 °C simply never reaches the bitter compounds.
🏆 JIBBI LITTLE — 2022 CHAMPION 🇦🇺 · the sifter
☕ 18 g💧 94 ml → 150 g🌡 90 °C🙃 inverted
grindKinu M47 at 3.8–4.0, then sifted. On the C5, go medium-fine and sift if you can.
0:00Inverted. 94 ml of water. 35 gentle stirs — count them.
1:30Flip. Press between 1:40 and 2:10.
finishDilute up to 150 g.
The pattern across six champions: lower temperature, a concentrate rather than a full cup, and dilution at the end. Almost none of them brew "normally." our own test: which one wins at home?
bigcupofcoffee.com/winning-aeropress-champion-recipes · aeropress.com/blogs/w-a-c-aeropress-recipes

Chapter III · Chemex

HOFFMANN'S CHEMEX


🏆 JAMES HOFFMANN — 2007 WORLD BARISTA CHAMPION (UK)
☕ 30 g coffee💧 500 g water ⚖ 60 g/L🌡 100 °C⚙ medium☕☕ serves 2
0:00Bloom with 80 g, swirl. (3-layer side of filter faces the spout!)
0:45Pour steadily up to 300 g over ~30 s.
1:15Pour to 500 g over ~30 s.
1:45Stir once clockwise, once counter-clockwise. Then a gentle swirl.
4:15Drawdown done. Remove filter, swirl the flask, serve.
Too fast? grind finer. Too slow? coarser. The Chemex forgives almost everything except impatience.
src: honestcoffeeguide.com/brew-recipes/james-hoffmann-chemex-recipe
19
Chapter III · Chemex

ICED CHEMEX


🧊 49TH PARALLEL ROASTERS — HOUSE GUIDE
☕ 40 g coffee🧊 250 g ice in the flask 💧 350 g hot water⚙ finer than usual
1.Weigh 250 g of ice straight into the Chemex. Filter + coffee on top.
2.Bloom with 80 g hot water.
0:50After the 45–50 s bloom, slowly pour the remaining water (350 g total).
3.Once drained, swirl until the ice stops melting.
4.Pour over fresh ice, stir, enjoy on the porch.
The ice is part of the recipe's water — that's why the dose is big and the grind fine. Instant iced clarity.
src: 49thcoffee.com/blogs/brew-guides/iced-chemex

Chapter IV · French Press

THE PATIENT PRESS


🏆 JAMES HOFFMANN — 2007 WORLD BARISTA CHAMPION (UK)
☕ 30 g coffee💧 500 g water 🌡 100 °C⚙ medium-coarse⏱ ~9:30 total
0:00Pour all 500 g of water in ~10 seconds. Walk away.
4:00Break the crust with a spoon — inhale, this is the best part.
4:30Skim off the floating grounds & foam with two spoons.
9:00After 5–8 more min of settling: rest the plunger just at the surface. Do NOT press down.
9:30Pour gently. Leave the last sip in the pot — that's where the silt lives.
The plunger becomes a sieve, not a piston. Cleanest french press you'll ever drink.
src: honestcoffeeguide.com/brew-recipes/james-hoffmann-french-press
22
Chapter IV · French Press

THE CLASSIC 4-MINUTE


☕ STUMPTOWN COFFEE — HOUSE GUIDE
☕ 56 g coffee💧 850 g water ⚖ ~1 : 15🌡 ~96 °C (205 °F)⚙ coarse, like breadcrumbs
0:00Start the timer, fill halfway — 450 g of water.
1:00Lid off, stir the grounds into the water. Top up to 850 g.
4:00Press — firmly, all the way down.
4:01Serve at once; decant what's left into a carafe so it doesn't stew.
The big-batch crowd-pleaser — heavier body than Hoffmann's, ready in half the time. Perfect when guests arrive in Baguio.

CHAPTER V

MOKA POT

24
Chapter V · Moka Pot

ULTIMATE MOKA POT


🏆 JAMES HOFFMANN'S TECHNIQUE
⚙ AeroPress-fine (coarser than espresso)💧 just-boiled water🔥 medium-low heat
1.Fill the base with hot, just-boiled water — up to the valve for light roasts, a little less for dark roasts.
2.Fill the basket to the top with coffee. Level it. No tamping.
3.Screw together (use a towel — the base is hot!) and set on medium-low heat, lid open.
4.Watch: coffee should flow out slow and syrupy, like warm honey.
5.At the first gurgle/sputter — off the heat. (Cooling the base under the tap stops extraction dead.)
Hot-water start = less metallic bitterness, since the coffee never gets cooked while the pot warms up.
src: espressoinsiders.com — James Hoffmann's moka pot recipe explained
25
Chapter V · Moka Pot

MOKA ON ICE


🧊 BEAN POET — BREW-OVER-ICE TRICK
☕ basket full, medium-fine💧 base ~half full 🧊 ~6 cubes in the TOP chamber🔥 medium-low
1.Fill the basket to the top; base chamber ~halfway with water.
2.Medium-low heat, lid open, watch the chimney.
3.Just before coffee emerges, drop the ice into the upper chamber (sugar on the ice now, if you like it sweet).
4.Brew lands straight on the ice — instant chill, no watery dilution.
5.Serve over fresh cubes, splash of milk if that's your thing.
Iced moka for hot Manila afternoons — the concentrate stays punchy because it cools on contact.
src: beanpoet.com/moka-pot-iced-coffee

Chapter VI · Cold Brew & Iced

OVERNIGHT CONCENTRATE


🏆 JAMES HOFFMANN'S METHOD
⚖ 1 : 10 (e.g. 100 g : 1 L)⚙ medium grind 🧊 fridge⏱ 12 h steep
1.Combine coffee + cold water at 1:10 in a jar. Stir to wet everything.
2.Lid on, into the refrigerator for 12 hours (14 h max — after that it just gets bitter).
3.Strain coarse first (sieve / cloth)…
4.…then pass through a paper filter for a clean, glossy concentrate.
5.Serve diluted 1:1 over ice. Keeps ~1 week chilled.
Perfect for the shop someday — batch it every night before closing, sell it every sunny Baguio afternoon.
src: calculate.coffee/cold-brew/james-hoffmann
28
Chapter VI · Cold Brew & Iced

ESPRESSO TONIC


🍋 THE CAFÉ SUMMER CLASSIC
☕ 1–2 shots espresso (or strong moka)🥤 tonic, well chilled ⚖ 1 : 3 espresso to tonic🧊 big clear cubes
1.Fill a tall glass with large ice cubes (small ones melt too fast).
2.Pour the tonic first — it keeps the bubbles alive and sets up the layers.
3.Pull the shots fresh.
4.Pour the espresso slowly over the back of a spoon so it floats on the tonic.
5.Garnish: strip of lemon, lime or orange peel — or a rosemary sprig. Stir at the table.
Bitter-sweet-fizzy and ridiculously photogenic — instant shop-menu material. Also works with cold brew concentrate instead of espresso.
src: methodicalcoffee.com — the perfect at-home espresso tonic

Chapter VI · Cold Brew & Iced

CÀ PHÊ SỮA ĐÁ


🇻🇳 VIETNAMESE ICED COFFEE — PHIN FILTER
☕ 20 g dark-roast robusta💧 80 g water @ 95 °C 🥛 20 g condensed milk⚙ medium-coarse⏱ ~5 min drip
1.Condensed milk first, straight into the glass. Phin filter on top, coffee in, level gently.
2.Bloom: pour 30 g of hot water, wait 40 seconds.
3.Add the remaining 50 g. Lid on.
~5:00Let it drip until the last drop falls. No rushing a phin.
5.Stir hard to marry coffee and milk, then pour over a glass packed with ice.
Robusta's punch is the whole point here — it stands up to the sweet milk. Feels right at home with Philippine barako too… experiment:

Chapter VI · Cold Brew & Iced

JAPANESE FLASH BREW


🇯🇵 KURASU KYOTO — HOUSE GUIDE
☕ 16 g coffee💧 150 g water @ 91 °C 🧊 70 g ice in the server⚙ medium-fine
0:00Ice in the server, V60 on top. Pour 40 g (each pour ~10 s).
0:40Pour +60 g (100 g total).
1:10Pour +50 g (150 g total) — nice and gentle, this pour just adjusts strength.
2:10Brew done. Swirl until every cube has melted, then serve over fresh ice.
Iced coffee in 2 minutes that keeps all the aroma cold brew loses — hot extraction, instant lock-in over ice. The shop's summer menu, sorted.

CHAPTER VII

KALITA WAVE

the flat bottom that forgives everything

Chapter VII · Kalita Wave

THE CHAMPION'S WAVE


🏆 JAMES McCARTHY — 2013 WORLD BREWERS CUP CHAMPION (USA)
☕ 24 g coffee💧 380 g water ⚖ ~1 : 16🌡 96 °C⚙ medium-coarse, fines sifted
0:00Pre-wet with 48 g — twice the dose. Let it bloom.
0:45Pour up to 190 g, keeping an even column of water above the grounds.
1:15Pour gently to 380 g — slow the flow right down (he used a flow-restricted kettle).
1:45Hands off. Let it draw down flat and even.
3:30Done — the bed should look like a level sandy beach.
He won the world title on this brewer — his edge was sifting out the fines before brewing. The flat bed extracts every particle the same.
src: timer.coffee/recipes/kalita-wave (champion recipe) · prima-coffee.com/learn (comparison)
33
Chapter VII · Kalita Wave

THE WAVE, FOUR WAYS

How the famous roasters ride the same three holes:
Onyx25 g / 400 g @ 95 °C — bloom 50 g + stir, then 110 g in circles, then four 60 g pours every 15 s. Done ~3:00.
Stumptown21 g / 375 g @ 96 °C — saturate 60 g + stir, spiral to 200 g by 1:00, pulse 25–50 g pours to 375 g. Done ~2:45–3:00.
G. Howell25–28 g / 390 g — metronome brewing: 65 g every 30 seconds, six times. Done 3:30.
5 Elephant14 g / 260 g — the tiny-brewer option: bloom 40 g + stir, all water in by 1:20.
The pattern: bloom ≈ 2× the dose, keep pours small & steady, respect the flat bed. Our house Wave:
src: prima-coffee.com/learn/article/brewing-guides/comparing-kalita-wave-recipes

Chapter VIII · Espresso

DIALLING IN — THE RECIPE


☕ THE "1:2 IN 30" RULE — every barista's starting point
☕ 18 g in💧 36 g out ⚖ 1 : 2⏱ 25–35 s🌡 ~93 °C⚙ fine as balance allows
1.Lock the dose: 18 g, weighed every time. Fill, distribute (WDT wiggle with a needle tool), tamp firm & level.
2.Pull to 36 g out — stop the shot on the scale, never by eye.
3.Check the clock: 25–35 s is the healthy window. Faster → grind finer. Slower → coarser.
4.Taste. Sour & sharp → finer grind, or stretch to 1:2.2. Bitter & harsh → coarser, or shorten toward 1:1.8.
5.Change one thing at a time, one step at a time. Log every shot →
Espresso is just three numbers: grams in, grams out, seconds. Everything else is romance.
src: espressoaf.com/guides/beginner.html (dialling-in basics)
36
Chapter VIII · Espresso

THE MILK BOARD

One double shot (~40 g out), five personalities — the milk is the costume:
macchiato40 g espresso + ~25 g milk — just “marked” with foam. Bold & tiny.
cortado40 g + ~55 g milk — near-equal partners, no foam theatrics. The balanced one.
flat white40 g + ~100 g milk, barely-there microfoam — silk with a strong coffee spine.
cappuccino40 g + ~100 g milk + ~1.5 cm foam cap — same bones as the flat white, airier hat.
latte40 g + ~230–240 g milk, ~1 cm foam — the mellow crowd-pleaser.
Going up the board = more milk, softer coffee. The shop menu writes itself from this one page.
src: coffeebros.com — espresso drinks explained (cappuccino vs latte vs flat white vs cortado)

SHOT DOCTOR

Symptoms → prescriptions, taped to every barista's machine:
gusherShot runs fast, pale & sour → grind finer.
chokerBarely drips, dark & bitter → grind coarser.
both?!Sour AND bitter at once = channeling. The fix isn't the grinder — it's puck prep: distribute, WDT, level tamp.
weakTastes good but thin → tighten the ratio (36 g → 32 g) or up-dose.
heavyGood but syrup-thick → stretch it: 1:2.5 lungo, or make it an americano.
Ratio cheat: ristretto 1:1.5 · espresso 1:2 · lungo 1:3

Chapter IX · Siphon

CLASSIC SIPHON


☕ SPRUDGE — THE STANDARD METHOD
☕ 35 g coffee💧 560 g hot water (~96 °C) ⚖ 1 : 16⚙ medium, like beach sand⏱ ~3:30
prepFilter chain hooked in the top chamber. Fill the bottom globe with hot water, flame on.
riseVapor pressure pushes the water up. Once it's (almost) all up top — add the 35 g of coffee.
0:00Gentle stir to fully saturate the grounds.
0:30Second gentle stir of the crust. Then leave it be.
2:00Kill the heat — the brew rushes back down through the cloth. Drawdown ≈ 1:30, with the famous final burp.
Adjust the grind by taste, not by the clock. A domed, even bed of grounds up top = you did it right.
src: sprudge.com/how-to-brew-with-a-siphon-coffee-maker-163518

🏆 CHANG WEI-SHIN — 2024 WORLD SIPHONIST CHAMPION (TAIWAN)

tempCommissioned a custom ceramic filter from a Taiwanese ceramic artist — it lowers the water temperature and improves circulation.

wisdom“Time pressure, as well as high temperatures, can combine to make coffee bitter.” — cooler & calmer wins.
Lesson for our siphon: heat is a throttle, not a switch — tame the flame after the rise, and the cup gets sweeter. Try a lower flame next brew:

Chapter X · Coffee Lore

A BRIEF HISTORY, PT. I

800sEthiopia. Goatherd Kaldi finds his goats dancing after eating red cherries; an abbot brews them to stay awake through night prayers.
1400sYemen grows the first crops; Sufi devotees drink it for long nights of devotion.
1500sThe first coffeehouses — qahveh khaneh — spread through Turkey, Persia, Egypt & Syria: music, chess, gossip, news.
1615Coffee lands in Venice; the clergy grumble until Pope Clement VIII tastes it — and blesses it.
1650sLondon's 300+ coffeehouses become “penny universities” — a penny buys coffee & the best talk in town.
1600sThe Dutch plant Java; mixed with Yemen's beans it becomes the first blend: Mocha Java.
1723Officer de Clieu shares his ship's water ration with one seedling → Martinique → 18 million trees in 50 years.
1773The Boston Tea Party turns America into a coffee country for good.
src: aboutcoffee.org — NCA, The History of Coffee
44
Chapter X · Coffee Lore

PT. II — COFFEE COMES HOME 🇵🇭

1740A Spanish Franciscan monk plants the first coffee tree in Lipa, Batangas.
1800sGroves spread through Batangas & Bulacan; by the mid-1850s Lipa is exporting to America and Australia, then Europe via the new Suez Canal.
1876First liberica — our kapeng barako — planted in Amadeo, Cavite.
1886The Philippines is the 4th largest coffee exporter on Earth. 🏆
1889–91Coffee rust strikes; in two years production collapses to one-sixth. The glory days end overnight.
todayOne of the few countries growing all four commercial species — arabica, robusta, excelsa, liberica — with Cordillera arabica (bourbon, typica & friends) leading the specialty revival. Our Baguio house is part of this story. ✎
src: philcoffeeboard.com — Philippine Coffee (history & regions)
45
Chapter X · Coffee Lore

FACTS FOR THE COUNTER

To be told over the brew bar, one per customer:
  • Coffee “beans” aren't beans — they're the seeds of a cherry-red fruit. You've been drinking pit juice, beautifully.
  • Lloyd's of London, the giant insurance market, started life as Edward Lloyd's coffeehouse in the 1600s.
  • Brazil's coffee empire allegedly began with seeds smuggled in a bouquet — a governor's wife's parting gift to Palheta (1727).
  • By the 19th century coffee ranked among the most sought-after commodities in the world.
  • The Philippines once out-exported almost everyone — 4th in the world, 1886 — and barako remains one of the rarest commercial coffees anywhere.
  • It all may have started because some goats danced.

Chapter X · Coffee Lore

BREW IT LIKE 1554 — THE CEZVE


🇹🇷 KURUKAHVECİ MEHMET EFENDİ — ISTANBUL HOUSE GUIDE
☕ 1 heaped tsp (~6 g) per cup💧 one demitasse of water per cup ⚙ extra-fine, like flour🍬 sugar optional — decide before brewing⏱ ~2 min
1.Measure the water with the serving cup, straight into the cezve.
2.Add coffee (and sugar, if taking). Stir well, then onto low heat.
3.Heat slowly. As the foam rises, lift off the heat and spoon a little foam into each cup.
4.Return for one more short rise, then pour gently down the side.
5.Serve with a glass of water — it wakes the mouth up for the coffee.
The foam is the pride of the cup — never walk away from a cezve. This is the drink the 1550s Istanbul coffeehouses were built on.
src: mehmetefendi.com — Turkish coffee with cezve brew guide

Chapter XI · Reference

THE GRIND DIAL — C5 ESP

Clicks counted from zero (burrs just touching). 50 clicks = 1 full turn, so 1.6.0 ≈ 80 clicks.
0–13EXTRA-FINE (0–200 µm) · flour — the cezve / Turkish (p. 43)
13–27FINE (200–400 µm) · table salt — espresso (p. 32)
27–40MEDIUM-FINE (400–600 µm) · fine sand — V60 classic, AeroPress, flash brew
40–53MEDIUM (600–800 µm) · beach sand — siphon, Chemex, filter
53–67MEDIUM-COARSE (800–1000 µm) · rough sand — the 4:6, Kalita, Hoffmann press
67–80COARSE (1000–1200 µm) · breadcrumbs — french press, cold brew
80–93EXTRA-COARSE (1200–1400 µm) · peppercorn bits — Kasuya's 10-pour (p. 6!), cold drip
Rule of thumb: ±3 clicks per bean & roast — darker roasts a touch coarser. Our sweet spots:
src: honestcoffeeguide.com coffee-grind-size-chart (µm bands) · beeancoffee.com C5 ESP ≈15 µm/click — click ranges computed from these, tune by taste

THE TASTING WHEEL

Chapter XI · Reference

HOW TO TASTE LIKE A CUPPER

1.Smell first — the dry grounds, then the wet crust. Half of “taste” is aroma.
2.Slurp loudly. Really. Spraying coffee across the whole palate is the professional move.
3.Start at the centre of the wheel: is it fruity? nutty? roasted? Don't hunt for “blackberry” right away.
4.Move outward one ring: fruity → berry or citrus? nutty → almond or chocolate?
5.Note texture & finish: silky? syrupy? clean? lingering? Then write it down here. ✎

Chapter XIII · The Numbers · Bataan

THE BOTTOM LINE

Everything below is computed in our live spreadsheet — change a number there and this page changes with it. Manual brew is the identity; a basic 1-group espresso machine is on the bar to meet the demand.
capital₱2.47 M full build on our own land — hard build ₱1.97 M + 10% contingency + ₱303k working capital
phase 1₱1.94 M for the leanest version that can legally open and still feel like the concept
the bar₱341,000 of that is the espresso bar — machine, its own grinder, tools, milk fridge, softener
break-even32 customers/day covers cash costs · 45/day is the TRUE break-even once depreciation & tax are counted
base case50 pax/day × ₱180 = ₱252,000/mo sales → ₱13,000/mo net profit (5.2%)
good case75 pax/day → ₱378,000/mo → ₱81,700/mo net (21.6%) — ₱981k a year
payback44 months full build · 34 months if we open Phase 1 first
⚠ THE ONE FINDING THAT MATTERS: if we LEASE the lot at ₱25k/mo, the same 50 customers a day leaves us losing ₱12,000 a month and true break-even jumps to 54/day. This concept only works on land we own.
Why? We're not fitting out a shop — we're developing land. The 200-m covered walk, comfort rooms, well & power are ₱517k of build that earns nothing directly. On rented ground you'd be gifting that to a landlord.
73
Chapter XIII · The Numbers

US vs A NORMAL PH CAFÉ

capitalthem ₱1.0–2.5 M · us ₱2.47 M — we are NOT cheaper. Salvage saves on the building; the land development spends it back.
coffee gearthem ₱250–600 k · us ₱663 k — but we get both bars: a 1-group commercial machine AND six manual stations. They spend the same and only get espresso.
furniturethem ₱80–150 k · us ₱94.5 k — bottom of the range, but it buys 40+ seats instead of 12.
gross marginthem 50–60% · us 63.5% ★ — still ahead, though the milk on the espresso bar costs us ~2 points.
staffthem 3–5 · us 2 — self-help brewing isn't a gimmick, it's the labour model. ⚠ past ~65 pax/day this becomes 3.
break-eventhem ≈37/day · us 32/day cash ★ — we survive a quiet Tuesday that would sink a mall café.
net marginthem 15–25% · us 5.2% at base, 21.6% at 75/day — the fixed costs are low, so profit swings hard on volume.
Read honestly: our margins beat the benchmark, our capital doesn't — and the base case is thin. We're buying an experience nobody else has, and paying for it in site works. The trade only works if the destination pulls people.
benchmarks: safc.com.ph PH café guide 2026 (budget, equipment, margins, break-even tables)

Chapter XIII · The Numbers

WHAT IT COSTS TO RUN

Every month, whether one customer shows up or a hundred:
labour₱60,964 — 2 staff × ₱590/day × 26 days + 13th month + employer SSS/PhilHealth/Pag-IBIG (₱1,364 each) + your own ₱25,000 draw
premises₱23,500 owned / ₱48,500 leased — power ₱16k (no aircon, but the espresso boiler idles hot ~₱4k), water, LPG, internet, + rent if leasing

TOTAL₱100,964/mo owned · ₱125,964/mo leased — plus ₱23,440 depreciation (not cash, but real)
The wage note: Region III minimum is ₱600/day non-agriculture, ₱590/day retail & service (Wage Order RBIII-26, effective 16 April 2026 — Bataan is covered). A retail/service shop with 10 or fewer workers may apply to the regional board for exemption; worth asking about, but budget the full rate.
The quiet advantage: an open-air shop has no aircon load. That alone is ₱8–15k a month a normal café pays and we don't — which is roughly what the espresso boiler costs us back.

Chapter XIII · The Numbers

WHAT EACH CUP EARNS — THE BREW BAR

Arabica at ₱1,042/kg incl. VAT (₱930 + VAT, 50 kg+ wholesale). 34% of our cups.
V60₱120 − ₱30.8 cost = ₱89.2 · 74.3%
AeroPress₱110 − ₱25.6 = ₱84.4 · 76.7%
french press₱180 for two − ₱47.3 = ₱132.7 · 73.7%
siphon ★₱190 − ₱34.0 = ₱155.9 · 82.1% — the best margin AND the best theatre
brew-your-own ★₱150 − ₱30.8 = ₱119.2 · 79.4% — and almost no barista time
barako₱90 − ₱19.4 = ₱70.6 · 78.4% — cheap, local, honest
cold brew₱120 − ₱23.5 = ₱96.5 · 80.4%
flash brew₱130 − ₱28.7 = ₱101.3 · 77.9%
Manual brew on its own runs ~24% COGS. It is the cheapest, highest-margin coffee there is — and the reason we teach it. But it is not what most walk-ins order.
The self-help arithmetic: Brew-Your-Own earns ₱119 on maybe 90 seconds of staff time. A latte earns ₱111 on three minutes. Per staff-minute, the brew bar wins — which is exactly why it stays.

beans 250 g₱450 − ₱275 = ₱175 · 38.9% — thinner, but it converts drinkers into brewers
water / soda₱40 − ₱25 = ₱15 · 37.5% — worst margin on the board. Don't let it grow
Blended across the whole mix: 63.5% gross margin, beverage COGS 25.8%. A milk-and-syrup café runs 55% / 35%.
Notice: even our worst espresso drink beats every food item. Coffee is the business; food just keeps people sitting.
78
Chapter XIII · The Numbers

★ DOES THE ESPRESSO MACHINE PAY?

The honest way to ask it: compare our shop against the same shop without a machine, and find how much extra traffic espresso must buy.
it costs₱375,100 of capital (₱341k + contingency), ₱4,000/mo more power, ₱4,060/mo more depreciation, ~2 points of beverage COGS — milk is the expensive liquid.
it earnsEspresso drinks price higher, lifting the average drink from ₱121.6 to ₱138.4. Most of the cost comes straight back.
net dragAt identical traffic — 50/day either way — the machine leaves us just ₱1,012/month worse off. That is the entire penalty.
the answerOne extra customer a day is worth ₱2,748/month net. So espresso must bring 0.4 of a customer a day to pay for itself.
★ THE VERDICT: the espresso bar needs less than one extra person per day to justify ₱375,100. If even one in ten of our visitors would have driven past a manual-only shop, it has already paid for itself many times over. Buy it.
The other way round: if a manual-only shop lost 35% of the traffic, it earns ₱44,620/month less than we do — a 143% annual return on the machine. That 35% is a judgement, not a measurement — but at 0.4 customers a day the decision doesn't hinge on it.
What it does NOT fix: espresso is barista-bound and does not scale on self-help. Past ~65 pax/day the bar needs a third pair of hands (+₱17,700/mo).
live sheet: EspressoCase tab · change the demand-loss cell and everything moves
79
Chapter XIII · The Numbers

THE FOUR PILLARS, IN PESOS

Our concept isn't decoration — each pillar does real work in the P&L:
1 · laid backPeople linger → fewer seat turns but a bigger ticket. We model ₱180 average vs the ₱150 benchmark. Cheap salvage seating means we can afford to give a table away for two hours. Risk: if the ticket lands at ₱150, true break-even moves from 45 to 54 a day.
2 · manual brewNot a restriction — a teaching floor. It holds 34% of cups at ~24% COGS instead of the espresso bar's 27%, worth about ₱4,000/mo in gross profit, and it is the only thing here a competitor can't copy by buying a machine. Espresso runs alongside it, not instead of it.
3 · self helpThe labour model. 2 staff instead of 3–4 ≈ ₱18,000/mo saved. Brew-Your-Own at ₱150 earns ₱119 with almost no barista minutes — our best product per staff-hour. Costs ₱25k to set up properly. ⚠ espresso partly undoes this: shots need a person.
4 · simple menu7 food items, shelf-stable, no chef, no pastry case. Waste modelled at 3% vs 5–8% typical ≈ ₱10,000/mo saved. Small kitchen = smaller build, faster service, easier permits. The espresso list stays at four drinks for the same reason — no syrups, no sauces, no frappé blender.
Add it up: the four pillars are worth roughly ₱32,000 a month versus running a conventional café — which is most of the difference between our base-case profit and zero.
80
Chapter XIII · The Numbers

THE SAFE-SIDE PACKAGE

Four changes. None of them touch the concept — each is a build decision, an accounting correction, or a product the concept already implies. Same 50 customers a day. No price rise assumed.
1 · phase 1+₱10,679/mo · −₱603,900 capital. Build Phase 1, depreciate over honest lives, keep the ₱148k Gabi V2. You still get the walkway, the hidden approach, the self-help stations, the espresso bar.
2 · workshops ★+₱15,772/mo. 2 weekend classes × 8 seats × ₱1,200. Not a new concept — pillar 3 with a price on it. The gear is already bought; marginal cost is ₱850 of beans and paper.
3 · the ₱250k+₱1,667/mo. The 8% option is computed on gross less ₱250,000. Our model was taxing every peso. ⚠ only while under ₱3M — see overleaf.
On depreciation: we were writing off concrete, a steel container and a deep well over 7 years — no accountant would book that. Split the lives (structures 15, equipment 7, furniture 5, smallwares 3) and the monthly charge falls from ₱23,440 to ₱12,762. Not one peso of cash changes. What changes is the break-even you plan against.
net profit₱13,019 → ₱41,137/mo
capital₱2,468,791 → ₱1,864,891
payback43.6 → 25.2 months
TRUE break-even45.3 → 35.6 pax/day
★ AND REMEMBER: the ₱41,137 is after paying yourself ₱25,000. Your actual monthly take is ₱66,137.

Chapter XIII · The Numbers

⚠ THE ₱3,000,000 CLIFF

Our base case is ₱252,000/mo = ₱3,024,000 a year. The VAT threshold is ₱3,000,000. We are ₱24,000 over the line before a single workshop is sold.
the rule₱3,000,000 of gross sales in a year — still ₱3,000,000 as of June 2026 (TRAIN Law RA 10963, NIRC §109(BB), RR 8-2018).
crossing itVAT registration becomes compulsory: 12% output VAT, quarterly filing, VAT invoices. And you lose the 8% flat option — reverting to graduated rates for the whole year.
why it bitesOur whole tax line is 8% of gross. If the shop performs as planned, it is wrong from year one. With workshops: ₱3,254,400. At 75/day: ₱4,536,000.
option APrice and register for VAT from day one — so you never raise the menu 12% in front of regulars.
option BDeliberately run under ₱3M — at ₱180 a head that caps us near 49 customers a day. A real business decision, not a loophole.
Not tax advice. Which regime costs less depends on deductible costs, and ours are high. Take the model to a Philippine accountant before registering — the election is made at registration and is awkward to undo.
Cheap insurance, no concept change:
  • Carry 4–6 months of working capital, not 3. A destination shop ramps slower.
  • Three quotes before signing. Site works, conversion and carpentry are ~45% of the build and none is quoted. A 20% miss is ₱180,000.
  • Open Phase 1, hold two quarters before spending the last ₱600k.
  • Track average ticket weekly. Everything rests on ₱180.
  • Test the ₱155 latte on 20 locals before printing menus.
  • Test the water before buying the boiler — ₱18k protects a ₱148–225k machine.
  • Budget the 3rd staff member at 65 pax/day. A plan, not a panic.
sweldoph.com 8% guide 2026 · lawyer-philippines.com VAT threshold
82
Chapter XIII · The Numbers

THE VERDICT & THE RISKS

The plan, in order:
  • Own the land. Non-negotiable. Leasing turns a ₱13k/month profit into a ₱12k/month loss.
  • Buy the espresso machine — the ₱148k one. It needs 0.4 extra customers a day to justify itself.
  • Open Phase 1 at ₱1.86 M, not the ₱2.47 M full build. Prove people come, then extend the walk and add the deck from cash flow.
  • Sell the workshops from month one. ₱15,772/month of profit from gear you already own — and the one thing no competitor can copy.
  • Settle the tax question BEFORE registering. We cross ₱3M in year one. See the previous page.
  • Plan for 36 a day. That is the safe-side true break-even. Anything above it is yours.
  • Never skip: 4–6 months of working capital, the ₱25k self-help stations, the ₱90k comfort rooms, the ₱18k softener.
What could still break it:
  • Nobody finds us. A hidden shop is a marketing problem disguised as a design idea. Budget the ₱5k/month and actually spend it.
  • Espresso pricing. ₱155 for a latte against Pickup's ₱85. We are betting on being a destination, not a commute stop.
  • Rain. Open-air + Philippine wet season = months where the courtyard can't seat.
  • The estimates. Site works, conversion and carpentry are ~45% of capex and none of it is quoted yet.
